title: App servers and autoscaling: more cooks for the rush
dek: Why app servers should keep no state, when a bigger machine beats more machines, and how autoscaling follows the day without failing the first minutes of a spike.

items: App servers run your code. Make them stateless: everything that must survive goes to a database, cache or object store, so any server can answer any request.
Scale up (a bigger machine) is simple but has a ceiling and one point of failure. Scale out (more machines behind a load balancer) has neither.
Size from measurements: requests a second one instance handles at a safe load, then divide your peak by that.
Autoscaling adds and removes instances to hold a target load, usually 50 to 70%. New instances take minutes to start, so a sudden spike still lands on the ones already running.
For a spike you know about (a sale, a match), scale out before it starts. Autoscaling is for the spikes you didn't plan.

body.x: Zotato's Order API runs as several identical copies. A request to place an order can land on any of them, and the next request from the same phone can land on a different one. That only works if no copy keeps anything important in its own memory or disk.

items: Orders, users and payments go to the database.
Logins are a signed token the app sends with every request, or a session kept in a shared store such as Redis.
Uploaded photos go to object storage, not the server's disk.
Work that takes long, like generating an invoice PDF, goes on a queue for workers.

body.x: Then a server can be added, replaced or killed at any time, and that is what makes everything else in this article possible.

Cooks in a restaurant kitchen. Each order is written on a ticket, not remembered by one cook, so any free cook can pick up the next ticket. When the rush comes you bring in more cooks; when a cook goes home, nothing is lost.

body.cap: Scale up: swap an m5.large (about 600 requests a second) for a c5.2xlarge (about 2,500). Scale out: keep the size and add copies behind a load balancer, 600 requests a second each. The Lab uses these sizes and numbers.

body.name: Scale up
body.what: Move to a machine with more CPU and memory.
body.use: Things that are hard to split, like a single database primary, and early on when one server is enough.
body.avoid: Relying on it for growth: the biggest machine is the limit, and that one machine going down takes everything with it.
body.ex: Zotato's first version ran on one server. Moving it to a bigger one bought months without changing any code.
body.like: Hiring one very fast cook. Great, until that cook is sick.
more: Bigger is not always more expensive per request. In the Lab's prices, four m5.large (2,400 requests a second) cost $0.404 an hour and one c5.2xlarge (2,500) costs $0.34. The reason to scale out anyway is that losing one of four servers costs a quarter of your capacity; losing the only one costs all of it.
Resizing usually means a restart, so it is a planned change, not something to do in the middle of a rush.

body.name: Scale out
body.what: Run more copies of the same server behind a load balancer.
body.use: Stateless app servers and workers: almost every web backend.
body.avoid: Servers that keep state locally; fix that first.
body.ex: The Order API runs 5 instances most evenings and 23 during the flash sale.
body.like: More cooks of the same skill, each taking the next ticket.
more: Keep at least two instances, in different availability zones, even when one would be enough for the load. That is what keeps the service up when an instance or a zone fails.

Everything behind the servers must keep up too. Twenty servers, each with a pool of 20 database connections, open 400 connections; many databases slow down or refuse long before that. Use a connection pooler, or smaller pools per server.

body.x: Measure one instance with a load test against realistic requests: how many requests a second it handles before response times climb. Then plan to run it at about 60% of that, which leaves room for uneven load, a slow dependency or one instance failing.

Zotato's evening peak is 1,600 requests a second. An m5.large handles about 600, so at 60% each takes 360: 1,600 ÷ 360 = 4.4, so 5 instances. The flash sale's 8,000 needs 23. At $0.101 an hour, 5 instances cost about $370 a month; 23 running all month would cost about $1,700.

Autoscaling runs the group between a minimum and a maximum number of instances and changes the count to follow the load. It saves money at night and adds capacity in the rush. But it reacts: it sees load rise, asks for instances, and they take a few minutes to boot and pass their health checks.

body.cap: The 8 pm flash sale with autoscaling at a 60% target. At 8:00 demand jumps from 1,600 to 8,000 requests a second. The group asks for 23 instances right away, but they take 4 minutes to boot, so for those 4 minutes everything above 3,000 a second fails. After the sale ends at 8:15, the group waits 15 minutes of low load before removing instances, so Zotato pays for idle ones until 8:30.

body.name: Target tracking
body.what: Keep a metric near a target, such as average CPU at 60% or requests per instance at 360. The autoscaler works out how many instances that needs.
body.use: Most web services. One number to choose.
body.avoid: Metrics that don't follow load. CPU says little about a service that mostly waits on other services; use requests per instance or queue length.
body.ex: The Order API tracks requests per instance with a target of 360.
body.like: Opening more ticket counters at the station when the queues get long. It helps, but a new clerk takes a few minutes to sit down.
more: Scaling out is quick to trigger; scaling in is deliberately slow (here, 15 minutes of low load). Removing instances too eagerly makes the group flap: add, remove, add again, with users paying for every cold start.

body.name: Scheduled
body.what: Set the size for a time: "from 7:50 pm, at least 24 instances".
body.use: Sales, launches, match days, the 9 am office rush: anything you can see coming.
body.avoid: Using it for normal daily ups and downs; target tracking already follows those.
body.ex: Zotato schedules 24 instances from 7:50 pm on sale days, so the sale starts on servers that are already warm.
body.like: A railway adding coaches to the trains before Diwali, not after the platform fills.
more: Predictive scaling, offered by some clouds, learns the daily pattern from past weeks and scales ahead of it. It helps with regular peaks, not with one-off events.

items: Bake the code into the machine image or container image, so a new instance doesn't install anything when it starts.
Keep start-up work small: load configuration and connect, and warm caches in the background.
Containers on a running cluster (Kubernetes, ECS) start in seconds instead of minutes, if the cluster has spare nodes. If it has to add nodes first, you are back to minutes.
Serverless functions (AWS Lambda, Cloud Run) scale per request and start fastest, but every new copy pays a cold start, and you trade control of the machine for a per-request price.
Headroom costs money: running at 60% means paying for 40% you don't use, most of the time. That is the price of not failing when traffic jumps.
Autoscaling is late by design. The first minutes of a sudden spike land on the instances already running.
Every layer behind the servers must scale too: database connections, cache capacity, and the rate limits of the services you call.
Set the maximum on purpose. Too low and autoscaling stops before the spike is covered; too high and a bug or an attack can run up a large bill.
Say the servers are stateless and name where state lives: database, cache, object storage, queue.
Do the sizing maths: peak requests a second ÷ what one instance handles at a safe load = instances, plus at least one spare across zones.
Mention autoscaling with its metric and target, and that it reacts in minutes.
For a known spike, say you would scale out ahead of it.
Check what scaling out does to the database: connections and queries grow with the number of servers.

body.x: At 8 pm Zotato's flash sale brings 8,000 requests a second for 15 minutes, five times the usual. New instances take 4 minutes to boot. Keep 99.9% of requests succeeding without blowing the budget.
